levels.title: The Pax Romana
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the Pax Romana and what peace made possible.
levels.summary: From Augustus to Marcus Aurelius, about 200 years of relative peace let trade, people and ideas move freely across the empire.

cards.headline: For about 200 years, most of the Roman world lived in peace.
cards.body: Not perfect peace, and not everywhere. But enough to change how people lived. So what did peace actually look like?

cards.headline: The Roman peace
cards.body: The Pax Romana, “Roman peace,” was a stretch of about 200 years of relative peace and stability across the empire. It began with Augustus and is usually dated from 27 BCE to 180 CE, when the emperor Marcus Aurelius died. Notice the start date: 27 BCE, the year Octavian became Augustus. The first emperor didn’t just bring peace. Peace was his brand.

cards.headline: What peace made possible
cards.body: Peace is good for business. With the seas and roads safe, trade flowed across the Mediterranean, the sea Romans called Mare Nostrum, “our sea.” Goods, people and ideas moved from one end of the empire to the other, and cities grew and prospered. Safe roads are boring. Boring is wonderful for business.

cards.fact: The Pax Romana wasn’t free of war.
cards.context: Fighting went on at the frontiers. What the peace meant was that the empire’s interior was largely spared. If you lived in a city deep inside the empire, war was news from far away. If you were a soldier on the frontier, the Pax Romana was something that happened to other people.

cards.headline: The peace: understood
learned: The Pax Romana lasted about 200 years
It ran from Augustus to Marcus Aurelius
Trade and cities flourished
Fighting went on at the frontiers

questions.prompt: Roughly how long did the Pax Romana last?
questions.explanation: The Pax Romana lasted about 200 years, from 27 BCE to 180 CE.

questions.prompt: How did the Pax Romana help trade?

options.label: Safe seas and roads let goods move freely
It closed the frontiers to foreign goods
It ended the use of coins

questions.explanation: Peace made travel safe, so trade, people and ideas moved freely.

questions.prompt: From Level 1: what did Romans call the Mediterranean at the heart of this trade?
questions.explanation: Romans called the Mediterranean Mare Nostrum, “our sea.”

levels.title: A City of Marble
levels.objective: After this level you can describe how Augustus rebuilt Rome and why buildings mattered politically.
levels.summary: Augustus restored temples, Agrippa built baths and the first Pantheon, and the Ara Pacis celebrated peace. Every building sent a message.

cards.headline: “I found Rome a city of brick and left it a city of marble.”
cards.body: That’s Augustus bragging, as the historian Suetonius tells it. The surprising part: all that marble was also a message.

cards.headline: Building an image
cards.body: By his own count in the Res Gestae, Augustus restored 82 temples in a single year. That’s more than one a week. Why so many? His buildings advertised his piety and the peace he had brought, linking his rule to Rome’s gods. Remember the pax deorum from Level 7, Rome’s peace with the gods? Every restored temple was a billboard: this man keeps Rome right with heaven.

cards.headline: A friend who built
cards.body: Agrippa, the admiral whose fleet won at Actium, was also a builder. He paid for major public works in Rome, including baths and aqueducts, and he built the first Pantheon. Visit the domed Pantheon today and you’re standing in a later rebuilding under the emperor Hadrian, not Agrippa’s original. Win the war, then build the baths. Not a bad friend to have.

cards.fact: The Ara Pacis, the Altar of Augustan Peace, was dedicated in 9 BCE.
cards.context: Its carvings show members of Augustus’ family in procession: a family portrait in marble. The message is hard to miss. Here is the peace, and here is the family that brought it.

cards.headline: Rome: rebuilt
learned: Augustus boasted of a city of marble
He restored 82 temples in one year
Agrippa built the first Pantheon
The Ara Pacis celebrated his peace

questions.prompt: How many temples did Augustus say he restored in a single year?
questions.explanation: In the Res Gestae, Augustus says he restored 82 temples in one year.

questions.prompt: Why did Augustus pour money into temples and monuments?

options.label: Rome had almost no stone buildings before him
options.rationale: He boasted of turning brick to marble.

options.label: To show his piety and tie his rule to the gods
To house the Senate’s new members
To prepare Rome for a siege

questions.explanation: His buildings advertised his piety and the peace he had brought.

questions.prompt: From Level 7: Roman religion aimed to keep the pax deorum. What was it?

options.label: A temple to the god of war
options.rationale: It was a relationship, not a building.

questions.explanation: The pax deorum was the peace between Rome and its gods, kept by correct ritual. Restoring temples served it.

levels.title: Virgil and the Aeneid
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what the Aeneid is and why Augustus's Rome valued it.
levels.summary: Virgil’s Aeneid follows the Trojan Aeneas to Italy. It gave Rome an epic to rival Homer’s, and Augustus’ family a heroic ancestor.

cards.headline: Rome’s greatest poem is about a refugee from a burning city.
cards.body: Not a conqueror, not a king. A man escaping the flames of Troy, guided by fate toward Italy. So why did Rome love this story so much?

cards.headline: The poem
cards.body: Virgil, who lived from 70 to 19 BCE, is widely regarded as the greatest poet of Augustan Rome. His Aeneid is an epic in 12 books, modeled on Homer’s Iliad and Odyssey. Its hero, the Trojan prince Aeneas, escapes burning Troy and, guided by fate, comes to Italy, where his descendants will found Rome. Rome’s great origin epic starts with a man who has lost his city.

cards.headline: A poem for Augustus
cards.body: Here’s why it suited the emperor so well. The Julian family, Caesar and Augustus included, claimed descent from Aeneas through his son Iulus. So Rome’s great epic doubled as Augustus’ family tree. And its hero is famous for pietas: dutiful devotion to the gods, his family and his country. Remember those 82 temples? Augustus was building the same image in marble.
cards.callout: Pietas: duty to gods, family and country

cards.fact: Virgil wanted the Aeneid burned.
cards.context: He died before finishing it and asked for the manuscript to be destroyed. Augustus had it published instead. Rome’s greatest poem survives because its author lost the argument.

cards.headline: The Aeneid: read
learned: Virgil was Augustan Rome’s great poet
The Aeneid follows Aeneas from Troy to Italy
Augustus’ family claimed Aeneas as ancestor
Aeneas stands for pietas, duty

options.label: Romulus
options.rationale: He comes much later in Rome’s story.

questions.explanation: The Aeneid follows the Trojan prince Aeneas from Troy to Italy.

questions.prompt: Why did the Aeneid suit Augustus so well?

options.label: It gave his family a heroic ancestor in Aeneas
It described his victory at Actium in full
It was written in Greek for the East

questions.explanation: The Julian family claimed descent from Aeneas, so Rome’s founding epic honored Augustus’ own line.

questions.prompt: From Level 2: Aeneas was one founding legend. Who, in the other, founded the city itself?
questions.explanation: Legend said the twins Romulus and Remus were raised by a wolf, and Romulus founded and named Rome.

levels.title: Months Named for Emperors
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the Julian calendar and how July and August got their names.
levels.summary: Caesar’s Julian calendar of 46 BCE gave us 365 days and leap years. Two months were renamed for him and for Augustus.

cards.headline: Two of your months are named after Roman rulers.
cards.body: Every summer, your calendar turns to July, then August. That’s Julius Caesar, then Augustus. How did two Romans end up on your wall?

cards.headline: Caesar fixes the year
cards.body: In 46 BCE Julius Caesar introduced the Julian calendar, on the advice of the astronomer Sosigenes of Alexandria. It had 365 days, plus a leap day every fourth year. Why the extra day? A year is about 365 and a quarter days long, and three ordinary years plus one leap year average exactly 365.25. Caesar only got two years with his new calendar. The Ides of March came in 44 BCE.

cards.headline: New names
cards.body: The Roman year once began in March, which solves a puzzle: Quintilis meant “fifth month,” and it was. It was renamed Julius, our July, in honor of Julius Caesar. Then, in 8 BCE, Sextilis was renamed Augustus, our August, in honor of Augustus. Adopted father and heir, side by side on every calendar you’ve ever owned.

cards.fact: The Julian calendar was slightly too long.
cards.context: By about 11 minutes a year. Tiny, but it added up, and the calendar drifted against the seasons. In 1582 Pope Gregory XIII replaced it with the Gregorian calendar we use today. Caesar’s calendar retired. His month didn’t.

cards.headline: The calendar: set
learned: Caesar’s calendar began in 46 BCE
It had 365 days and a leap day
July honors Caesar and August honors Augustus
The Gregorian calendar replaced it in 1582

questions.explanation: Quintilis was renamed Julius, our July, in Caesar’s honor.

questions.prompt: Why does the Julian calendar add a leap day every fourth year?

options.label: To honor Augustus with an extra day
To make every month the same length
To fit the Roman festival cycle
A year is about 365 and a quarter days long

questions.explanation: Three 365-day years and one 366-day year average 365.25 days.

questions.prompt: From Level 40: Caesar didn’t live long with his new calendar. When was he killed?
questions.explanation: Caesar was killed on the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BCE, two years after his calendar began.

levels.title: Teutoburg Forest
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the disaster in the Teutoburg Forest and how it fixed the Rhine frontier.
levels.summary: In 9 CE Arminius led three legions under Varus into an ambush and destroyed them. Rome gave up on Germany and held the Rhine.

cards.headline: In 9 CE three Roman legions marched into a German forest. They never came out.
cards.body: And the man who led them to their doom was someone their general trusted.

cards.headline: The ambush
cards.body: In 9 CE, Germanic warriors led by Arminius destroyed three Roman legions under the governor Varus in the Teutoburg Forest. The shock was who Arminius was. He had served with the Roman army, and Varus trusted him. Arminius led him into an ambush. Remember Level 29: a legion had roughly 4,000 to 5,000 infantry. Three of them is some 12,000 to 15,000 soldiers, lost in one ambush.

cards.headline: The river becomes a border
cards.body: The disaster changed the map. Rome gave up its plans to conquer Germany east of the Rhine, and the river became a lasting frontier. How do we know where it happened? Archaeologists believe the battlefield lies near Kalkriese in Germany, where Roman weapons and coins have been found. One ambush in a forest, and a river became a border.

cards.fact: “Quintilius Varus, give me back my legions!”
cards.context: According to the historian Suetonius, Augustus cried out these words after hearing of the disaster. The sole master of the Roman world, and there was one thing he couldn’t get back.

cards.headline: The frontier: fixed
learned: Arminius ambushed Varus in 9 CE
Three legions were destroyed
The Rhine became the frontier
Augustus mourned his lost legions

options.rationale: He led a slave revolt in Italy.

questions.explanation: Arminius, who had served with the Roman army, led the ambush.

options.label: Rome abandoned the province of Gaul

questions.explanation: Rome gave up conquering Germany east of the Rhine, which became a lasting frontier.

questions.prompt: From Level 29: a legion had roughly 4,000 to 5,000 infantry. About how many were in three?
questions.explanation: Three legions of 4,000 to 5,000 infantry each make roughly 12,000 to 15,000 soldiers.

levels.title: Milestone: From Republic to Empire
levels.objective: After this level you can trace Rome's path from republic to empire and explain what changed and what stayed.
levels.summary: From the Gracchi to Augustus, violence and loyal armies turned the Republic into one-man rule that kept the Republic’s old forms.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. How did a republic become an empire?
cards.body: In about a century, Rome went from Tiberius Gracchus to an emperor, and it kept its Senate the whole way. Let’s trace the road.

cards.headline: Same forms, new master
cards.body: The Republic didn’t end with a sign on the Senate door. Its forms stayed, the Senate and consuls included, so one man’s rule still looked like a republic, while real power passed to him. Even the word emperor gives the game away. It comes from imperator, a title soldiers gave to a victorious commander. Not a word from the Senate or the voters. A word from the army.

cards.headline: The road to one-man rule: follow the armies

levels.title: Tiberius
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the reign of Tiberius and the problem of succession.
levels.summary: Tiberius, Augustus’ adopted stepson, ruled from 14 to 37 CE, much of it from Capri. Rome had no rule for choosing the next emperor.

cards.headline: Following Rome’s first emperor came with no instructions.
cards.body: Augustus built a brand-new job and never wrote down how to hand it on. So who gets it next, and who decides?

cards.headline: The heir who was left standing
cards.body: Augustus had no surviving son. He chose other successors first, and they died. So he adopted his stepson Tiberius as heir, and Tiberius became emperor on Augustus’ death in 14 CE, ruling until 37 CE. Here’s the catch: Rome never had a fixed law of succession. Each emperor had to choose his own heir, often by adoption. Imagine a family business where every owner rewrites the will from scratch.

cards.headline: Ruling from an island
cards.body: In his later years Tiberius withdrew to the island of Capri and ruled from there. Remote work, Roman style. But an absent boss leaves an empty office in Rome. Sejanus, commander of the Praetorian Guard, grew more and more powerful while Tiberius was away, until Tiberius had him executed in 31 CE. The man guarding the emperor had become the problem.

cards.fact: The Praetorian Guard was the emperor’s bodyguard, stationed in Rome itself.
cards.context: Soldiers that close could protect the emperor. As Sejanus showed, the man commanding them could also grow too strong. Keep an eye on this guard. It matters again in the very next level.

cards.headline: Tiberius: met
learned: Augustus adopted his stepson Tiberius
Tiberius ruled from 14 to 37 CE
He withdrew to Capri
Rome had no law of succession

His nephew, the son of Octavia

options.label: The Senate elected emperors every year

questions.explanation: Without a law of succession, each emperor had to pick an heir, and rivals could contest the choice.

questions.explanation: Augustus called himself princeps, and his successors inherited the role.

levels.title: Caligula
levels.objective: After this level you can separate what is known about Caligula from later rumor.
levels.summary: Caligula, “little boot,” began popular in 37 CE and became autocratic. His own guard killed him in 41 CE. Many tales about him are hostile rumor.

cards.headline: Most of what you’ve heard about Caligula was written by people who hated him.
cards.body: So what can we actually trust? Start with a nickname, end with a murder, and read the gossip in between with care.

cards.headline: Little Boot
cards.body: Gaius became emperor in 37 CE, but everyone knows him by a nickname. As a child he lived in his father’s army camp, wearing a small soldier’s uniform, and the soldiers called him Caligula, “little boot.” Imagine ruling an empire under your childhood nickname. He was popular at first. Then his rule turned autocratic and extravagant.

cards.headline: Consider the source
cards.body: Here’s the trouble with Caligula’s legend: most accounts of him come from later writers who were hostile to him. So historians treat the wildest stories with caution. Take the famous one about his plan to make his horse a consul. It may be a joke, or an exaggeration. Before you ask whether a story is true, ask who wrote it.
cards.callout: Ask who wrote a story, and why

cards.fact: Caligula was murdered by officers of his own guard in 41 CE.
cards.context: Remember the Praetorian Guard from Level 51, the bodyguard stationed in Rome? The men meant to protect the emperor ended his reign after just four years. This part of the story isn’t gossip.

cards.headline: Caligula: sifted
learned: Caligula means “little boot”

His guard murdered him
Hostile sources shape his legend

options.rationale: Close, but it was about his footwear.

options.label: He banned all writing during his reign

questions.explanation: Hostile later writers had reasons to exaggerate, so their wildest claims need caution.

questions.prompt: From Level 51: which force, meant to protect the emperor, killed Caligula?
questions.explanation: Officers of the Praetorian Guard, stationed in Rome, murdered Caligula in 41 CE.

levels.title: Claudius Conquers Britain
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Claudius's reign and the invasion of Britain.
levels.summary: The guard made Claudius emperor in 41 CE. The scholar few took seriously invaded Britain in 43 CE, where Boudica later rose in revolt.

cards.headline: The emperor nobody took seriously conquered a land Caesar only raided.
cards.body: Julius Caesar went to Britain twice and left. It took a man his own family kept out of public life to make it Roman.

cards.headline: The unlikely emperor
cards.body: After Caligula’s murder, the Praetorian Guard made his uncle Claudius emperor in 41 CE. Nobody had bet on him. Claudius had a limp and a stammer, and his family had kept him out of public life. He was a scholar who wrote histories, now lost. As emperor he leaned on freedmen, formerly enslaved people, as powerful officials. The relative they hid became the man in charge.

cards.headline: Britain becomes Roman
cards.body: In 43 CE Claudius launched the invasion of Britain, and this time the island became a Roman province. Not everyone there agreed. In about 60 CE Boudica, queen of the Iceni, led a revolt that burned London before the Romans crushed it. The quiet scholar had won a province, and the province fought back.

cards.fact: Caesar had raided Britain twice, in 55 and 54 BCE.
cards.context: Caesar visited. Claudius moved in. His invasion came nearly a century later, and this time Rome stayed.

cards.headline: Britain: conquered

He was a scholar kept out of public life
He invaded Britain in 43 CE

levels.title: Nero and the Great Fire
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the Great Fire of Rome and Nero's reputation.
levels.summary: Nero became emperor at 16. After the fire of 64 CE he blamed the Christians and built a palace on the ruins. His death in 68 CE ended Augustus’ line.

cards.headline: Rome burned for six days, and people have blamed Nero ever since.
cards.body: But what did he actually do? The real story has a teenage emperor, a scapegoat and a palace. It has no fiddle.

cards.headline: The teenage emperor
cards.body: Nero, Claudius’ adopted son, became emperor in 54 CE at the age of 16. Picture a 16-year-old handed the Roman world. It ended badly. Facing revolt, Nero took his own life in 68 CE, and with him ended the Julio-Claudian dynasty, the family line of Augustus. The family business had run out of family.

cards.headline: The Great Fire
cards.body: In 64 CE a great fire burned in Rome for six days. Of the city’s 14 districts, three were destroyed and seven more badly damaged. According to the historian Tacitus, Nero blamed the Christians in Rome and had many of them executed. Then, on land the fire had cleared, he built a vast palace, the Golden House. Not a great look for the man in charge.

cards.fact: Nero did not fiddle while Rome burned.
cards.context: That story is a later legend. The fiddle did not yet exist, and Tacitus says Nero was away at Antium when the fire began. It’s hard to play an instrument nobody has invented, in a city you’re not in.

cards.headline: Nero: judged

Rome burned for six days in 64 CE
He blamed the Christians

questions.explanation: The instrument was invented much later, and Tacitus places Nero at Antium when the fire started.

questions.explanation: Nero was Claudius’ adopted son and succeeded him in 54 CE.

levels.title: The Year of the Four Emperors
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what happened in 69 CE and what it revealed about imperial power.
levels.summary: In 69 CE four men ruled in turn, each backed by an army. Vespasian won, proving that emperors could be made far from Rome.

cards.headline: In a single year, Rome had four emperors.
cards.body: Nero was dead, and Augustus’ family line with him. So who got to rule now? Whoever had an army behind him.

cards.headline: 69 CE
cards.body: After Nero’s death in 68 CE came 69 CE, the Year of the Four Emperors. Galba, Otho, Vitellius and Vespasian each held power in turn. Four names, one calendar. What they had in common was an army: each claimant was backed by one. That was the year’s real lesson. The legions could make emperors, and they could unmake them.

cards.headline: The winner
cards.body: The last man standing was Vespasian, a general commanding in Judaea. He won the civil war and founded the Flavian dynasty. Looking back at Nero’s fall, the historian Tacitus named what it had exposed, a secret of empire: an emperor could be made somewhere other than Rome. The top job no longer had to be decided in the capital. It could march in from far away.

cards.fact: Vespasian came from a family of modest rank.
cards.context: No old Roman nobility, no famous ancestors. What he had was an army, and in 69 CE that counted for more than an ancient name.

cards.headline: The year: survived
learned: Four emperors ruled in 69 CE
Each was backed by an army

levels.title: The Flavians and the Colosseum
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the Flavian dynasty and the building of the Colosseum.
levels.summary: Vespasian and his sons Titus and Domitian ruled until 96 CE. They built the Colosseum on the grounds of Nero’s palace.

cards.headline: The Colosseum stands where an emperor’s private lake used to be.
cards.body: Nero’s palace grounds became Rome’s most famous arena. The family that did it was the one that won Level 55.

cards.headline: A family of soldiers
cards.body: Vespasian’s new dynasty was a family business. In 70 CE his son Titus captured Jerusalem and destroyed its Temple. Titus later succeeded his father as emperor, and was followed by his brother Domitian. Domitian’s rule was harsh, and it ended with his murder in 96 CE. Father, son, second son, and the Flavians were done.

cards.headline: The Colosseum
cards.body: Vespasian began the Colosseum, and Titus opened it in 80 CE with games that lasted 100 days. It could hold about 50,000 spectators. The location was part of the point. It stood on the site of a lake in the grounds of Nero’s Golden House, giving the land back to public use. One emperor’s private lake became everybody’s day out.

cards.fact: The Colosseum is also called the Flavian Amphitheatre.
cards.context: It’s named after the dynasty that built it, though Romans mostly just called it the amphitheatre. The name Colosseum came later, probably from a colossal statue of Nero nearby. The Flavians built over Nero’s lake, and Nero still ended up naming their arena.

cards.headline: The Colosseum: opened
learned: Titus took Jerusalem in 70 CE
The Colosseum opened in 80 CE
It held about 50,000 people
It was built on Nero’s palace grounds

questions.explanation: The Colosseum held about 50,000 spectators.

It gave a hated ruler’s land back to the people

It was the only flat land left in Rome

options.label: A temple to the god Janus

levels.title: Pompeii and Vesuvius
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the eruption of Vesuvius and why Pompeii is so valuable to historians.
levels.summary: In 79 CE Vesuvius buried Pompeii and Herculaneum. The ash that killed the towns preserved them, and Pliny the Younger described it all.

cards.headline: A volcano destroyed a town, and by burying it, saved it for us.
cards.body: The ash that ended life in Pompeii also sealed the town up, like a time capsule nobody meant to pack.

cards.headline: The eruption
cards.body: In 79 CE Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried two towns, Pompeii and Herculaneum. Titus was emperor, a year before he opened the Colosseum. Remarkably, we have a written account. Pliny the Younger described the eruption in letters to the historian Tacitus. His uncle, Pliny the Elder, died trying to rescue people.

cards.headline: A town frozen in time
cards.body: Pompeii was buried under several meters of ash and pumice. A disaster for its people, a gift for historians: the ash preserved buildings, paintings and everyday objects. Even the walls still talk. They carry painted notices and scratched graffiti, including election slogans. Imagine a town where the campaign posters never came down. Together it all gives historians a rare snapshot of ordinary Roman town life.

cards.fact: Plaster casts show victims in their final positions.
cards.context: The victims’ bodies left hollows in the ash. In the 1800s, excavators poured plaster into those hollows, and the casts recorded their final positions. The ash kept the town, and in a way it kept its people too.

cards.headline: Pompeii: uncovered
learned: Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE
It buried Pompeii and Herculaneum
Pliny the Younger described it
The ash preserved a whole town

questions.explanation: The eruption buried Pompeii and Herculaneum.

questions.prompt: Why is Pompeii so valuable to historians?

options.label: It was the empire’s richest and largest city
Its people wrote the first Roman history

It was the only town the eruption spared

questions.explanation: Buried under ash, Pompeii kept buildings, paintings, objects and graffiti that usually disappear.

questions.prompt: From Level 56: which emperor, who opened the Colosseum a year later, ruled when Vesuvius erupted?
questions.explanation: Titus was emperor in 79 CE and opened the Colosseum in 80 CE.

levels.title: Trajan's Empire at Its Largest
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Trajan's conquests and the empire at its greatest extent.
levels.summary: Trajan, born in Spain, conquered Dacia and pushed into Mesopotamia. In 117 CE the empire reached its greatest extent.

cards.headline: The empire reached its largest size under an emperor born in Spain.
cards.body: Rome’s biggest moment on the map came under the first emperor from outside Italy.

cards.headline: The best emperor
cards.body: Trajan, born in Spain, was the first emperor from outside Italy. He ruled from 98 to 117 CE, and the Senate gave him the title Optimus, “the best.” That’s not a nickname, it’s a job review. Every emperor so far had come from Italy. Now the empire’s own provinces could produce its ruler, and the Senate rated him top of the class.

cards.headline: Pushing the edges
cards.body: Trajan ruled during the Pax Romana, but that peace had edges. The empire’s interior was largely peaceful while fighting went on at the frontiers, and that’s where Trajan worked. He conquered Dacia, roughly modern Romania, in two wars ending in 106 CE. Then he pushed east as far as Mesopotamia. In 117 CE the empire reached its greatest extent. Rome would never be bigger on the map.

cards.fact: Trajan’s Column tells the story of the Dacian wars in stone.
cards.context: A spiral band of carvings winds up the column in Rome from base to top, showing the campaigns scene by scene. It’s a war report you read by walking in circles.

cards.headline: The empire: at its largest
learned: Trajan was born in Spain
He ruled from 98 to 117 CE
He conquered Dacia
The empire peaked in 117 CE

options.label: Rome was sacked by the Gauls again

questions.explanation: In 117 CE, after Trajan’s conquests, the empire was at its largest.

levels.title: Hadrian and His Wall
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Hadrian consolidated the frontiers and built his wall.
levels.summary: Hadrian gave up some conquests, toured the frontiers and fortified them. His wall ran about 118 km across northern Britain.

cards.headline: Hadrian’s answer to an empire too big to grow: guard its edges.
cards.body: Trajan left the empire at its biggest. His successor, Hadrian, went the other way: not how to grow it, but how to hold it.

cards.headline: Holding, not growing
cards.body: Hadrian, Trajan’s successor, ruled from 117 to 138 CE, and one of his big moves was handing land back: he gave up some of Trajan’s eastern conquests. Then he went to check on the rest. He spent much of his reign traveling through the provinces, inspecting armies and frontiers. An emperor doing site visits. In Rome he rebuilt the Pantheon, first built by Agrippa, as the domed building still standing today.

cards.headline: The wall
cards.body: Hadrian’s Wall, begun in 122 CE, ran about 118 km across northern Britain. It had small forts about every Roman mile, and larger forts along its length. That’s not a garden fence. It’s a frontier with a small fort every Roman mile, and it says out loud where the empire stops.
cards.callout: Hadrian’s Wall: begun 122 CE, about 118 km long

cards.fact: Hadrian was the first emperor regularly shown with a full beard.
cards.context: He loved Greek culture, and he wore it on his face: the beard was in the Greek style. Even his portraits tell you where his heart was.

cards.headline: The frontier: guarded
learned: Hadrian ruled from 117 to 138 CE
He gave up some conquests
His wall crossed northern Britain
He rebuilt the Pantheon

He meant to invade all of Scotland next

questions.prompt: From Level 46: who built the first Pantheon, which Hadrian rebuilt?
questions.explanation: Agrippa built the first Pantheon; the domed building standing today is Hadrian’s rebuilding.

levels.title: Checkpoint: The Five Good Emperors
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the era of the Five Good Emperors, ending with Marcus Aurelius.
levels.summary: From 96 to 180 CE, emperors chosen by adoption gave Rome its steadiest era. Marcus Aurelius passed power to his son Commodus, and it ended.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 finale. Five emperors in a row who ruled well. Then it ended.
cards.body: Remember Rome’s missing rule for choosing the next emperor? For most of a century, Rome found a way around it. Then a father handed power to his son.

cards.headline: Choosing the best
cards.body: Nerva, Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius, who ruled from 96 to 180 CE, are known as the Five Good Emperors. None of the first four left a surviving son, so each passed power to an adopted adult heir. (Even ancient writers doubted Trajan really adopted Hadrian before he died.) The historian Edward Gibbon called it the time when the human race was most happy and prosperous. Marcus Aurelius’ death in 180 CE is also where the Pax Romana is usually said to end.

cards.headline: The philosopher emperor
cards.body: The last of the five, Marcus Aurelius, was a Stoic philosopher. He wrote his private reflections, the Meditations, while on campaign: philosophy homework, done at the front. His reign had troubles too. A deadly epidemic, the Antonine Plague, swept the empire from about 165 CE. Then came the handover. Marcus was succeeded by his own son, Commodus, whose disastrous reign ended the era. After four chosen heirs, a son simply inherited.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 complete

His son Commodus ended the era

levels.title: A Day in the City
levels.objective: After this level you can describe daily life in the city of Rome, from apartment blocks to the forum.
levels.summary: Perhaps a million people crowded into Rome. Most rented rooms in risky apartment blocks; the rich lived in houses built around an atrium.

cards.headline: A million people, one city, and most of them had no bath at home.
cards.body: So where did all those Romans actually live? Mostly stacked on top of each other.

cards.headline: Apartment life
cards.body: By the time of Augustus, Rome had perhaps around 1 million people, the largest city in the Western world. Most of them lived in insulae: crowded apartment blocks several stories high, usually without running water or private baths. The upper floors were the cheapest, and fire and collapse were constant dangers. Do the math: the cheaper your room, the more floors between you and the street when a fire broke out.

cards.headline: Houses and the Forum
cards.body: If you were rich, you skipped the stairs. Wealthy Romans lived in a domus, a private house built around an open hall called the atrium. Public life, for everyone, centered on the Forum, the once-marshy valley you met in Level 3. It packed temples, law courts, markets and platforms for speeches into one place. Picture a town square that was also the courthouse, the church and the mall.

cards.fact: Augustus gave Rome a force of night-time firefighters.
cards.context: He created the vigiles, freedmen who fought fires and patrolled the streets at night. He also capped new buildings at about 20 meters high. Rome’s apartment blocks finally had a ceiling.

cards.headline: The city: explored
learned: Rome had perhaps a million people
Most lived in insulae
The rich lived in a domus
The Forum was the center of public life

levels.title: Slavery in Rome
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how slavery shaped Roman society and what freed slaves could become.
levels.summary: Enslaved people, taken by war, piracy and birth, did every kind of work. Many were freed, and a citizen’s freed slave became a citizen.

cards.headline: In Rome, a doctor, a teacher and a miner could all be enslaved.
cards.body: Slavery reached into every corner of Roman life. So did something more surprising: a way out.

cards.headline: Property under the law
cards.body: Enslaved people made up a large share of the population of Roman Italy. War, piracy and trade fed the system, and a child born to an enslaved mother was enslaved too. Under Roman law an enslaved person was property, with no legal rights of their own. In the eyes of the law, a human being could be owned like a cart or a plow.

cards.headline: Every kind of work
cards.body: Enslaved people did every kind of work. Some dug in mines or labored on farms; others ran households. Some were teachers, doctors and secretaries, so the person teaching a rich family’s children could legally be property. But the story didn’t always end there. Romans often freed enslaved people, a practice called manumission.

cards.fact: A citizen’s freed slave usually became a Roman citizen.
cards.context: Their children had full rights. Freedom could even lead to power: the emperor Claudius relied on freedmen, formerly enslaved people, as powerful officials. Owned in one generation, fully Roman in the next.

cards.headline: Slavery: understood
learned: Enslaved people were legally property
War, piracy and birth fed slavery
Manumission freed many
Freed slaves of citizens became citizens

questions.explanation: Manumission was the freeing of an enslaved person, which Romans did often.

options.rationale: Their children gained full rights, not office.

questions.explanation: A person freed by a citizen usually became a citizen, and their children had full rights.

levels.title: Bread and Circuses
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the grain dole and public games and why rulers provided them.
levels.summary: Rome fed about 200,000 citizens with free grain and staged huge free games. A poet mocked it as “bread and circuses.”

cards.headline: A Roman poet said his people wanted only two things: bread and circuses.
cards.body: He wasn’t paying them a compliment. So what were the bread and the circuses, and who was handing them out?

cards.headline: Free grain
cards.body: The bread was real. Rome gave free grain to many citizens living in the city, and under Augustus about 200,000 people received it. That’s a lot of mouths to feed. Much of that grain came from Egypt, a province under the emperor’s personal control. The emperor didn’t just run the city. He ran its pantry.

cards.headline: Free games
cards.body: The circuses were real too. Public games, ludi, began as religious festivals and grew into huge free entertainments. Worship had become a show. Who paid? Emperors and politicians, who funded games and food to win popularity and keep the city calm. Crowd control, served with a side of spectacle.

cards.fact: “Bread and circuses” was a complaint.
cards.context: The poet Juvenal said the Roman people, who once handed out commands, now wanted only these two things. His jab: citizens who used to give the orders had settled for free food and shows.

cards.headline: Bread and circuses: explained

About 200,000 received it

levels.title: Gladiators
levels.objective: After this level you can separate the reality of gladiator fights from popular myth.
levels.summary: Gladiator fights began as funeral games. Most fighters were enslaved or condemned, fought in set types, and were often spared.

cards.headline: Thumbs down meant death? Probably not the way the movies show it.
cards.body: The real arena was stranger, and often less deadly, than the film version.

cards.headline: Who fought
cards.body: Gladiator fights probably began as funeral games to honor the dead, first recorded in Rome in 264 BCE. So Rome’s bloodiest show started as a way to mourn. Most gladiators were enslaved people, prisoners of war or condemned criminals. But some free men volunteered. Yes, a few people chose this job.

cards.headline: How they fought
cards.body: Gladiators fought in types with set equipment. The retiarius, armed with a net and trident, faced the helmeted secutor: a matchup, not a brawl. And gladiators were expensive to train, so many fights did not end in death. A beaten fighter could be spared. Nobody wants to lose an expensive investment in one afternoon.

cards.fact: No one knows exactly what the thumb meant.
cards.context: Roman writers mention a “turned thumb” deciding a gladiator’s fate, but its exact meaning is unknown. So when a movie emperor jabs his thumb down with total confidence, he knows more than historians do.

cards.headline: Gladiators: unmasked

Most gladiators were enslaved or condemned
They fought in set types
Many beaten fighters were spared

levels.title: Chariot Racing
levels.objective: After this level you can describe chariot racing, the Circus Maximus and the racing factions.
levels.summary: The Circus Maximus held about 150,000 fans. Four color factions raced four-horse chariots seven laps, and rivalries could turn into riots.

cards.headline: Rome’s biggest crowds didn’t watch gladiators. They watched chariots.
cards.body: Rome had a venue that made the Colosseum look small. And its fans turned out to be more than spectators.

cards.headline: The Circus Maximus
cards.body: The Circus Maximus, Rome’s great racetrack, could hold about 150,000 spectators, about three times the Colosseum’s 50,000. A standard race was seven laps around the central barrier, the spina. The most prestigious races used quadrigae: chariots pulled by four horses. Seven laps, four horses, and a crowd the size of a city.

cards.headline: Reds, Whites, Blues and Greens
cards.body: Charioteers raced for four factions, the Reds, Whites, Blues and Greens, and each faction had passionate fans. Sound familiar? It’s the ancient version of wearing your team’s colors. A charioteer who won often enough could become rich and famous. The first sports celebrities drove at a gallop.

cards.fact: Racing fans nearly toppled an emperor.
cards.context: In 532 CE, fans of two factions, the Blues and the Greens, rioted together in Constantinople. The Nika revolt nearly toppled the emperor Justinian. When sports fans can shake a throne, they’re a political force. Not bad for a day at the races.

levels.title: The Baths
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what Roman baths were like and why they mattered socially.
levels.summary: Cheap, heated public baths had hot, warm and cold rooms. Romans went to exercise, talk and do business, not just to wash.

cards.headline: For a Roman, the bath was the gym, the café and the office.
cards.body: Getting clean was almost the least of it.

cards.headline: Hot, warm, cold
cards.body: Large public baths, thermae, had rooms at three temperatures: the hot caldarium, the warm tepidarium and the cold frigidarium. The heat came from below. In the hypocaust, hot air from furnaces flowed under raised floors and up through the walls. Cold tiles on bare feet were not a Roman bather’s problem.

cards.headline: Why Romans went
cards.body: Remember Level 61: most Romans lived in apartment blocks without private baths. The public baths did far more than fill that gap. Romans exercised, talked, did business and relaxed there, and entry was cheap. The Baths of Caracalla, opened in the 3rd century CE, could serve about 1,600 bathers at a time. That’s a very crowded office.

cards.fact: Romans cleaned themselves without soap.
cards.context: Instead, bathers oiled their skin and scraped it clean with a curved metal tool, the strigil. Oil on, scrape off, and the dirt went with it. No bubbles, but it worked.

cards.headline: The baths: visited
learned: Baths had hot, warm and cold rooms
The hypocaust heated the floors
Baths were social centers

levels.title: What Romans Ate
levels.objective: After this level you can describe what rich and poor Romans ate, including garum.
levels.summary: Most Romans ate grain, oil, wine and beans; the rich reclined at banquets. Almost everyone loved garum, a fermented fish sauce.

cards.headline: One of Rome’s most popular flavors came from fermented fish.
cards.body: Before you wince, see what else was on the table, and what definitely wasn’t.

cards.headline: Everyday food
cards.body: Most Romans lived on grain, eaten as porridge or bread, with olive oil, wine, vegetables and beans. Remember the apartment dwellers from Level 61? Many had no kitchen at home, so street counters called thermopolia sold them hot food. Ancient Rome had takeout.

cards.headline: Fish sauce and feasts
cards.body: Garum, a fermented fish sauce, was one of the most popular seasonings in the Roman world. Coastal factories, especially in Spain, made it, and clay jars called amphorae carried it around the empire. Fish sauce went everywhere Rome did. The rich dined differently: they held dinner parties in the triclinium, reclining on couches around a table. Dinner, lying down, with fish sauce.

cards.fact: No Roman ever ate a tomato.
cards.context: Tomatoes, potatoes and maize came from the Americas more than a thousand years later. A Roman cookbook attributed to Apicius survives, with many recipes that use fish sauce and not one tomato. Fish sauce, yes. Tomato sauce, no.

levels.title: Latin, the Language That Lived On
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Latin spread and became the Romance languages.
levels.summary: Latin spread west with soldiers and settlers, and spoken Latin became Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese and Romanian.

cards.headline: The Western Empire fell. Its language kept going.
cards.body: Latin didn’t vanish with Rome. It grew up into languages people still speak.

cards.headline: From Latium to the West
cards.body: Latin started small, in Latium, the region around Rome. It was the language of the Latins, the first Romans. As Rome grew, Latin spread through the western provinces with soldiers, settlers and officials. The East was different: Greek stayed the common language there. Rome ruled the East, but the East kept talking Greek.

cards.headline: Latin’s children
cards.body: Everyday spoken Latin, often called Vulgar Latin, didn’t stay put. It gradually developed into the Romance languages, including Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese and Romanian. English isn’t one of them, but a large share of its vocabulary comes from Latin, much of it through French. So even this sentence is partly Roman.

cards.fact: Latin outlived the empire that spread it.
cards.context: It remained the language of the Western Church, law and scholarship for centuries after the Western Empire fell. And Romanian descends from the Latin spoken along the lower Danube, including Dacia, the land Trajan conquered. Scholars still debate exactly where it first took shape.

levels.title: Roman Women
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the rights and roles of Roman women, and their limits.
levels.summary: Roman women couldn’t vote or hold office, and early law gave them male guardians. Yet many owned property, ran businesses and wielded influence.

cards.headline: She couldn’t vote, but she might run a business or be the emperor’s wife.
cards.body: Roman women lived with hard limits, and some found real power anyway.

cards.headline: Limits
cards.body: Start with the limits. Roman women could not vote or hold political office. Under early Roman law a woman needed a male guardian for legal matters, though the rule weakened over time. Girls from elite families were often married in their early to mid teens, usually to older men; most other girls probably married in their late teens. And remember the paterfamilias from Level 8? A daughter grew up under his legal power.

cards.headline: Wealth and influence
cards.body: Now the other side. Many Roman women owned property, ran businesses and inherited wealth. Influence didn’t need an office, either: Livia, the wife of Augustus, was one of the most influential people in Rome. Women also served as priestesses. The Vestal Virgins tended the sacred fire of Vesta, which was never allowed to go out. No vote, but Rome’s sacred fire was in their hands.

cards.fact: Julius Caesar’s daughter was simply called Julia.
cards.context: Roman daughters usually took a feminine form of the family name: Julius became Julia. Compare her father’s three-part name from Level 8, Gaius Julius Caesar. He got a small family tree; she got one word.

cards.headline: Roman women: met
learned: Women could not vote or hold office
Early law required a male guardian
Many owned property and businesses
Livia was hugely influential

questions.prompt: Which of these could Roman women NOT do?
questions.explanation: Roman women could not vote or hold political office.

questions.prompt: How was Livia influential without holding office?

options.label: She was the wife of Augustus
She led the Senate
options.rationale: Women couldn’t sit in the Senate.

questions.explanation: As Augustus’ wife, Livia was one of the most influential people in Rome.

questions.prompt: From Level 8: who held legal power over a Roman daughter in her father’s family?

options.label: Her eldest brother
options.rationale: The oldest living male held power.

questions.explanation: The paterfamilias, the oldest living male, held legal power over his children.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Everyday Rome
levels.objective: After this level you can connect housing, work, food, entertainment and religion into a picture of daily life.
levels.summary: Cramped homes pushed Roman life into public spaces. Patrons, household gods, free grain and games held the city together.

cards.headline: Chapter 7 finale. Put a whole Roman day together.
cards.body: You’ve seen where Romans lived, ate, washed, worshiped and cheered. Now see why so much of it happened in public.

cards.headline: Life in public
cards.body: Put the chapter’s pieces side by side. Rome had grand public spaces, such as baths, forums and arenas, and crowded, risky housing for most people. Those two facts explain each other. Because homes were cramped, much of Roman life happened in public: in the streets, baths, forums and arenas. The city was everyone’s living room.

cards.headline: The ties that bound
cards.body: Relationships held the city together too. Many Romans were clients of a wealthy patron: each morning they greeted him, and in return he offered help and protection. At home, households honored the Lares and Penates, guardian spirits of the home and its food store, at a household shrine. Favors out in the city, small gods at home.
cards.callout: Patron and client: help in return for a morning greeting

cards.headline: Chapter 7 complete
learned: Most Romans lived in cramped insulae
Life happened in public spaces
Clients served wealthy patrons
Grain, games and baths kept the city calm

questions.prompt: What were insulae?
questions.explanation: Insulae were apartment blocks several stories high, where most Romans lived.

questions.prompt: What did Roman law consider an enslaved person to be?

options.label: A member of the patron’s family
A soldier owed to the state

questions.explanation: Under Roman law an enslaved person was property, with no legal rights of their own.

questions.prompt: Why did so much Roman life happen in public places?

options.label: The law banned gatherings at home
Private homes were taxed by the hour

questions.explanation: With most people in small insulae, the baths, forums and streets became everyone’s living room.

questions.prompt: What did a client give a wealthy patron?

options.label: A morning greeting, in return for help and protection
A share of every harvest by law
options.rationale: Clients greeted their patron; there was no such tax.

options.label: Military service in his legion
options.rationale: Clients greeted their patron; it wasn’t army service.

questions.explanation: Clients greeted their patron each morning in return for help and protection.

questions.prompt: Chapter 7 recap: how did grain, games and baths help keep Rome calm?

options.label: They were paid for by the poor
They gave city people food, fun and space
They kept citizens out of the Forum
They trained citizens for the legions

questions.explanation: Free grain, games and cheap baths made life in a crowded city bearable, and won rulers popularity.

levels.title: All Roads Lead to Rome
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Roman roads were built and why they mattered.
levels.summary: Layered, drained and as straight as the land allowed, over 80,000 km of main roads carried armies first, then everyone else.

cards.headline: Rome laid more than 80,000 km of main roads. Who were they for?
cards.body: Not for sightseeing. The answer explains why Romans built them so carefully, one layer at a time.

cards.headline: Built like a layer cake
cards.body: A major Roman road wasn’t just paving stones laid on dirt. It was stacked in layers: a foundation of large stones, then gravel or rubble, then paving stones on top. It ran as straight as the ground allowed, and it was cambered, curved slightly, so rainwater drained off instead of sitting in puddles. Next time you notice the gentle hump in the middle of a street, you’re looking at a Roman idea.
cards.callout: Camber: a slight curve that sheds water

cards.headline: Built for marching
cards.body: Roman roads were built first for the army. A straight, solid, well-drained road let legions march quickly. Remember the Via Appia from Level 19, begun in 312 BCE to move armies south? That was the model. But once a road existed, everyone used it: traders, officials and the imperial post. Built for boots, used by everyone.

cards.fact: Roman roads came with distance markers: milestones.
cards.context: Milestones along the roads marked distances in Roman miles, each 1,000 paces long. So a traveler could count down the stones to the next town, the way you watch the signs tick down on a highway today.

cards.headline: The roads: traveled
learned: Roads were built in layers
They were cambered to drain rain
They served the army first
Milestones measured Roman miles

questions.prompt: Why were Roman roads cambered?

options.label: To mark the edge of each province
So carts could pass each other

questions.explanation: A slight curve let rainwater run off instead of pooling and breaking the road.

questions.prompt: Who were Roman roads built for first?

options.label: Merchants carrying grain to Rome
options.rationale: They came to use them too.

options.label: The army, to move legions quickly

questions.explanation: Roads let legions march quickly, and trade and officials followed.

questions.prompt: From Level 19: what was Rome’s first great road?
questions.explanation: The Via Appia, begun in 312 BCE, was built to move armies quickly to the south.

levels.title: Aqueducts
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how aqueducts carried water to Roman cities using gravity.
levels.summary: Aqueducts ran on a gentle downhill slope, mostly underground. By the 3rd century CE, 11 of them fed the city of Rome.

cards.headline: Rome brought water into the city without a single pump.
cards.body: No engines, no waterwheels. Just one force that never takes a day off.

cards.headline: Downhill all the way
cards.body: An aqueduct was a very long, very gentle slide. Water flowed by gravity along a steady downhill slope from springs in the hills. And the famous arches? They’re the exception. Most of an aqueduct’s length ran underground or at ground level. Arches only carried it across valleys, where the ground dropped away but the slope had to stay steady. Keep the slope steady, and the water keeps coming.

cards.headline: Water for a city
cards.body: Rome’s first aqueduct, the Aqua Appia, was built in 312 BCE by Appius Claudius, the same man who began the Appian Way. Roads and water in the same year: busy man. More followed, and by the 3rd century CE, 11 aqueducts supplied the city. Water mattered so much that Rome had a water commissioner. Around 97 CE that was Frontinus, who wrote a whole book about the aqueducts.

cards.fact: The Pont du Gard still stands in southern France.
cards.context: It’s one of those valley-crossing bridges: three tiers of arches, about 49 m high, all to keep the water on its gentle downhill slope.

cards.headline: Water: delivered
learned: Aqueducts ran on gravity
Most of their length was hidden
Rome’s first was built in 312 BCE
11 aqueducts fed Rome

questions.prompt: What moved water through a Roman aqueduct?
questions.explanation: Aqueducts ran on a gentle, steady downhill slope, so gravity did the work.

questions.prompt: Why did aqueducts need arches in some places?

options.label: To show off the emperor’s wealth
To keep the slope steady across valleys
To hold up the city walls

questions.explanation: Arches carried the channel across dips in the land, keeping the gentle slope unbroken.

questions.prompt: From Level 19: Appius Claudius built Rome’s first aqueduct. What else did he begin?
questions.explanation: Appius Claudius began both the Aqua Appia and the Via Appia in 312 BCE.

levels.title: Roman Concrete
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what made Roman concrete so durable.
levels.summary: Lime and volcanic ash made a concrete that set underwater and shaped domes. Lumps of lime even helped it heal its own cracks.

cards.headline: Romans built harbors out in the sea, with concrete that set underwater.
cards.body: How do you make something harden while it’s soaking wet? The secret came out of a volcano.

cards.headline: Ash and lime
cards.body: Roman concrete mixed lime with volcanic ash, called pozzolana, plus chunks of rock or brick. The ash is named after Pozzuoli, near Naples, where it was dug. It was the key ingredient: concrete made with it could set even underwater. So Romans could do something that sounds like a terrible idea, putting fresh concrete into the sea, and build harbors there.
cards.callout: Pozzolana: volcanic ash from near Naples

cards.headline: New shapes, hidden core
cards.body: Concrete didn’t just survive the sea. It let Romans build arches, vaults and domes on a scale never seen before. You’d rarely notice it, though. Walls were usually faced with brick or stone, so the concrete core was hidden from view. Rome showed you the neat outfit and kept the muscle underneath.

cards.fact: Roman concrete could repair itself.
cards.context: A 2023 study found that lumps of lime in the mix could react with water to seal cracks, helping the concrete last. Water, the enemy of most buildings, was helping these ones heal.

cards.headline: Concrete: set
learned: Concrete mixed lime and volcanic ash
It set underwater
It made domes and vaults possible
Lime lumps helped seal cracks

questions.prompt: What volcanic ingredient went into Roman concrete?
questions.explanation: Roman concrete mixed lime with volcanic ash called pozzolana.

questions.prompt: Why could Romans build harbors out in the sea?

options.label: They drained the sea with pumps

questions.explanation: Concrete made with volcanic ash set even underwater.

questions.prompt: From Level 46: Augustus boasted he found Rome a city of brick and left it a city of what?
questions.explanation: Augustus claimed he left Rome a city of marble; much of it was marble facing over concrete and brick.

levels.title: The Pantheon
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the Pantheon and its record-breaking dome.
levels.summary: Hadrian’s Pantheon has the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world, lit only by its oculus. As a church it survived intact.

cards.headline: The largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world was built by the Romans.
cards.body: Remember the volcanic concrete from Level 73? This is what it could do at full stretch.

cards.headline: A ball inside a building
cards.body: Pantheon means “of all the gods.” The building standing today is Hadrian’s rebuilding of Agrippa’s first Pantheon. Its dome, about 43 m across, is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. And the proportions are perfect: the height from the floor to the top of the dome equals its diameter. So a complete sphere 43 m wide would fit inside, resting on the floor.

cards.headline: Light and lightness
cards.body: Look up and there’s a hole in the roof. The oculus, about 8 m wide, is the building’s only source of natural light. The dome itself slims down as it rises: it gets thinner toward the top, and lighter stone was mixed into the concrete higher up. Less weight up high means less weight pressing down on everything below.
cards.callout: Oculus: the open “eye” at the top

cards.fact: The Pantheon survived by changing religion.
cards.context: In 609 CE the temple “of all the gods” became a Christian church, which helped it survive intact. New job, same building.

cards.headline: The Pantheon: entered
learned: Pantheon means “of all the gods”
Its 43 m dome is still a record
The oculus is its only light
It survived as a church

questions.prompt: What does the name Pantheon mean?
questions.explanation: Pantheon means “of all the gods.”

questions.prompt: How did the Pantheon’s dome change as it rose?

options.label: It got thicker toward the top
options.rationale: It got thinner as it rose.

options.label: It switched to solid marble
options.rationale: It stayed concrete, with lighter stone mixed in.

options.label: It got thinner, with lighter stone higher up
It stayed the same all the way up
options.rationale: It thinned and lightened as it rose.

questions.explanation: The dome gets thinner toward the top, and lighter stone was mixed into the concrete higher up.

questions.prompt: From Level 59: which emperor rebuilt the Pantheon as it stands today?

options.label: Augustus
options.rationale: His friend Agrippa built the first one.

questions.explanation: Hadrian rebuilt the Pantheon first built by Agrippa.

levels.title: Running the Provinces
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how governors, taxes and local elites ran the provinces.
levels.summary: Governors ran provinces, split by Augustus between the Senate and himself. Taxes came from a census, and local elites did most of the work.

cards.headline: Rome ran a vast empire with surprisingly few officials.
cards.body: So who did all the work? Mostly, other people.

cards.headline: Who got which province
cards.body: Augustus split the provinces in two. Peaceful ones got governors chosen by the Senate. Frontier provinces, the ones with armies, were run by his own deputies. Notice which half he kept: the half with the soldiers. Either way, every province paid taxes on land and on people, and a census counted them for taxation. Being counted by Rome meant being charged by Rome.

cards.headline: Local help
cards.body: Here’s the few-officials secret. Rome relied on local elites to govern their own cities and collect taxes. Under the Republic, tax collection had often been contracted out to private companies of publicani instead, and they were notorious for abuses. Handing a for-profit company the job of squeezing your subjects: what could go wrong?

cards.fact: Pontius Pilate was a provincial governor.
cards.context: He was the Roman prefect who governed Judaea from 26 to 36 CE. A name most people know, in a job most people never think about.

cards.headline: The provinces: run
learned: Governors ran the provinces
Augustus kept the armed provinces
A census set the taxes
Local elites did most of the governing

questions.prompt: Who collected taxes for Rome in many Republican provinces?
questions.explanation: Tax collection was often contracted out to publicani, notorious for abuses.

questions.prompt: Why did Augustus keep the frontier provinces for himself?

options.label: That was where the armies were
The Senate refused to govern them

questions.explanation: Frontier provinces held the legions, and controlling them meant controlling the army.

questions.prompt: From Level 30: which was Rome’s first province?
questions.explanation: Rome’s provinces began with Sicily, taken after the First Punic War.

levels.title: Becoming Roman
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Roman citizenship and how it spread to all free people in 212.
levels.summary: Citizenship brought legal privileges. It spread to Italy, then to towns, soldiers and individuals, until Caracalla gave it to almost all free people in 212 CE.

cards.headline: In 212 CE, one emperor made almost every free person a Roman citizen.
cards.body: For centuries, citizenship had been something you were granted or earned. What made it worth having?

cards.headline: What citizenship meant
cards.body: Roman citizens had legal privileges, such as the right to appeal to Rome and protection from certain punishments. Think of it as a passport that doubled as a shield. According to the Book of Acts, Paul of Tarsus, a Roman citizen, used exactly that shield: his right to appeal to the emperor.

cards.headline: How it spread
cards.body: Italy got it the hard way. During the Social War of 91–88 BCE, Rome granted citizenship to its Italian allies, which helped end the revolt. After that it spread through the provinces by grants to towns, to individuals and to soldiers. Non-citizen soldiers, the auxiliaries, received it after about 25 years of service. And as Level 62 showed, a person freed by a Roman citizen usually became a citizen too.

cards.fact: In 212 CE Caracalla made almost every free person a citizen.
cards.context: After centuries of grants, one town, one veteran at a time, being Roman became a status shared across the whole empire. The members’ club had opened its doors to nearly everyone.

cards.headline: Citizenship: granted
learned: Citizens had legal privileges
Italians gained citizenship in the Social War
Auxiliaries earned it by service
Caracalla extended it in 212 CE

questions.prompt: Which emperor granted citizenship to almost all free people in 212 CE?
questions.explanation: Caracalla’s grant of 212 CE made almost all free inhabitants citizens.

questions.prompt: How could an auxiliary soldier become a citizen?

options.label: By paying a fee in Rome

questions.explanation: Auxiliaries, non-citizen soldiers, received citizenship after about 25 years of service.

questions.prompt: From Level 62: how else could an enslaved person become a citizen?

options.label: By being freed by a Roman citizen
By fighting well in the arena
By moving to the city of Rome
By learning to read and write Latin

questions.explanation: A person freed by a Roman citizen usually became a citizen.

levels.title: Roman Law
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the key ideas of Roman law and how they reached modern legal systems.
levels.summary: Jurists developed Roman law for a thousand years after the Twelve Tables. Justinian’s code carried it into the law of much of the world.

cards.headline: If you live in France or Brazil, your law has Roman roots.
cards.body: The trail runs through Roman lawyers’ opinions and one emperor’s giant collection.

cards.headline: Lawyers who shaped the law
cards.body: Rome first wrote its laws down around 450 BCE, in the Twelve Tables. Then its legal experts, the jurists, wrote opinions that developed and explained the law. Some of their ideas now feel like common sense. Take the burden of proof: it rests on the person who makes a claim, not on the one who denies it. If your neighbor says you owe him money, he has to prove it. You don’t have to prove you don’t.
cards.callout: Burden of proof: whoever claims must prove

cards.headline: Justinian’s code
cards.body: In the 6th century CE the emperor Justinian had Roman law collected into the Corpus Juris Civilis, the “body of civil law.” That code shaped the civil law systems used across continental Europe, Latin America and many other countries. So a court in Paris or São Paulo still runs on ideas an emperor had collected about 1,500 years ago.

cards.fact: Legal English is full of Latin.
cards.context: Many legal terms are Latin words, such as alibi, which means “elsewhere.” So “I have an alibi” really just says “I was elsewhere.”

cards.headline: The law: laid down
learned: Jurists developed Roman law
The claimant bears the burden of proof
Justinian’s code collected the law
Civil law systems grew from it

questions.prompt: Which emperor had Roman law collected into the Corpus Juris Civilis?
questions.explanation: Justinian had Roman law collected in the 6th century CE.

questions.prompt: Under the Roman rule on burden of proof, who must prove a claim?
questions.explanation: The burden of proof rests on whoever makes the claim, not on the one who denies it.

questions.prompt: From Level 15: when did Rome first write down its laws, in the Twelve Tables?
questions.explanation: Around 450 BCE Rome wrote down its laws in the Twelve Tables, displayed in the Forum.

levels.title: Money and Trade
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Roman coins, trade routes and the economy of the Mediterranean.
levels.summary: The silver denarius carried the emperor’s face everywhere. Amphorae carried wine, oil and fish sauce, and traders reached India.

cards.headline: In Rome there is a hill made entirely of broken jars.
cards.body: To see how it got there, follow the money, and the olive oil.

cards.headline: Coins with a message
cards.body: The denarius, a silver coin, was the standard Roman coin for centuries. It was also a tiny billboard: coins carried the emperor’s portrait and short messages, spreading his image across the empire. Every time you paid, you saw the boss. Then came the catch. Over time emperors reduced the silver in the denarius, and by the 3rd century CE it held very little. Same coin, same face, less and less silver.

cards.headline: Goods on the move
cards.body: Wine, olive oil and fish sauce moved around the Mediterranean in amphorae, clay jars made for shipping. Think of them as Rome’s cardboard boxes. And trade didn’t stop at the sea’s edge: Roman traders sailed to India, and Chinese silk reached Rome through many middlemen along the Silk Road.

cards.fact: Monte Testaccio is an artificial hill.
cards.context: It’s made of fragments of millions of broken olive oil amphorae, piled up in Rome itself. Picture how much olive oil that was, and then remember it’s only the empties.

cards.headline: Trade: mapped
learned: The denarius was Rome’s silver coin
Coins spread the emperor’s image
Amphorae carried oil, wine and garum
Trade reached India and China

questions.prompt: What was the denarius?
questions.explanation: The denarius was the standard silver coin of Rome for centuries.

questions.prompt: Why did emperors put their portraits on coins?

options.label: To prove the coins were gold
Because the law required a face
To spread their image across the empire

questions.explanation: Coins passed through countless hands, carrying the emperor’s face and messages everywhere.

questions.prompt: From Level 67: which fish sauce was shipped around the empire in amphorae?
questions.explanation: Garum was made in coastal factories, especially in Spain, and shipped in amphorae.

levels.title: Life on the Frontier
levels.objective: After this level you can describe forts, soldiers and communities on the Roman frontier.
levels.summary: Auxiliaries held standard forts along the limes. Towns grew beside them, and the Vindolanda tablets let us read their letters.

cards.headline: At a fort in northern Britain, a commander’s wife sent a birthday invitation.
cards.body: Life on the edge of the empire wasn’t all marching and watching. So who actually lived out there?

cards.headline: Forts on the limes
cards.body: The fortified frontier of the empire was called the limes. Much of it was held by auxiliaries, non-citizen soldiers recruited from the provinces: the same soldiers who received Roman citizenship after about 25 years (Level 76). Their forts followed a standard plan: a rectangle with rounded corners, four gates and a headquarters building at the center. Seen one Roman fort? You could find your way around the next.

cards.headline: Towns beside the forts
cards.body: Where there were soldiers, other people followed. Civilian settlements grew up beside frontier forts, with traders, craftsmen and soldiers’ families. On Hadrian’s Wall, small forts stood about every Roman mile, with larger forts along its length. A frontier, it turns out, was also a neighborhood.

cards.fact: We can read letters written on the frontier.
cards.context: At Vindolanda, a fort near Hadrian’s Wall, archaeologists found more than a thousand wooden writing tablets. Among them is the invitation from the start of this level, from one commander’s wife to another. It’s everyday frontier life, in the frontier’s own words.

cards.headline: The frontier: held
learned: The limes was the fortified frontier
Auxiliaries held much of it
Towns grew beside the forts
Vindolanda preserved frontier letters

questions.prompt: What was the limes?
questions.explanation: The limes was the fortified frontier of the empire.

questions.prompt: Why are the Vindolanda tablets so valuable?

options.label: They list every emperor in order
They are the only Latin writing found

questions.explanation: Letters like a birthday invitation reveal ordinary life that official histories leave out.

questions.prompt: From Level 76: what did auxiliaries receive after about 25 years of service?
questions.explanation: Non-citizen auxiliaries received Roman citizenship after about 25 years.

levels.title: Checkpoint: How Rome Held an Empire
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how roads, law, citizenship, the army and trade held the empire together.
levels.summary: Roads, a shared army, citizenship, law and trade held the empire together, and Roman ways spread through the provinces.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 finale. How do you hold together an empire from Britain to Egypt?
cards.body: Not with soldiers alone. You’ve already met most of the answer in this chapter.

cards.headline: More than force
cards.body: Rome held its empire together with roads, a shared army, citizenship, law and trade, not by force alone. It also ran its provinces with few officials: local elites ran their own cities and collected the taxes. And in 212 CE almost every free person became a citizen. The strongest glue wasn’t fear. It was citizenship and shared law: being Roman.

cards.headline: Becoming Roman
cards.body: Historians call the spread of Roman language, culture and ways of life in the provinces Romanization. You could see it: towns across the West built forums, baths and amphitheaters on the Roman model. You could hear it too, as Latin spread through the western provinces with soldiers, settlers and officials. In the East, Greek stayed the common language.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 complete
learned: Roads, army, law and trade held the empire
Local elites ran their cities
Citizenship spread to nearly all
Romanization spread Roman ways

questions.prompt: What did Roman milestones measure?
questions.explanation: Milestones marked distances in Roman miles of 1,000 paces.

questions.prompt: What happened in 212 CE?

options.label: Rome was sacked by the Gothic army

Hadrian’s Wall was begun in the north

questions.explanation: In 212 CE Caracalla granted citizenship to almost all free inhabitants.

questions.prompt: How did Rome govern so much with so few officials?

options.label: Local elites ran their own cities

The emperor visited every city yearly

questions.explanation: Rome relied on local elites to govern their cities and collect taxes.

questions.prompt: What is Romanization?

options.label: The conquest of Italy by Rome
The spread of Roman roads only

questions.explanation: Romanization is the spread of Roman language, culture and ways of life in the provinces.

questions.prompt: Chapter 8 recap: which pair did most to bind the empire’s peoples to Rome?

options.label: Gladiator games and chariot races
options.rationale: They entertained, but didn’t bind the provinces.

options.label: Aqueducts and baths
options.rationale: They served cities, not the whole empire.

questions.explanation: Citizenship and a shared law gave provincials a stake in Rome, alongside roads, trade and the army.

levels.title: The Crisis of the Third Century
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the chaos of the third century, when emperors rose and fell rapidly.
levels.summary: From 235 to 284 CE, more than 20 emperors came and went, an emperor was captured, and the empire split in three before Aurelian reunited it.

cards.headline: More than 20 emperors in about 50 years. Most of them were murdered.
cards.body: Remember 69 CE, when the legions learned they could make and unmake emperors? For half a century, they did it again and again. Becoming emperor was a promotion with a very short life expectancy.

cards.headline: Everything at once
cards.body: From 235 to 284 CE, the Crisis of the Third Century, the empire suffered civil wars, invasions, plague and economic trouble, all at the same time. Even the money went bad. Emperors had kept reducing the silver in the denarius until the coin held very little, and prices soared. Imagine every new batch of coins holding a little less of the metal that made them worth anything. That was Roman money in the third century.

cards.headline: An emperor taken prisoner
cards.body: Then came the low point. In 260 CE the emperor Valerian was captured by the Persian king Shapur I. No Roman emperor had ever been taken prisoner by a foreign enemy before. The empire itself came apart, too. For a time it split into three: a breakaway Gallic Empire in the west, Rome in the middle, and Palmyra under Queen Zenobia in the east. One empire, three maps.

cards.fact: Aurelian put the pieces back together.
cards.context: In the 270s the emperor Aurelian reunited the three pieces into one empire. He also built new walls around Rome itself. A reunited empire whose capital needed fresh walls: that is the third century in a single picture.

cards.headline: The crisis: survived
learned: The crisis ran from 235 to 284 CE
More than 20 emperors ruled
Valerian was captured by Persia
Aurelian reunited the empire

questions.prompt: Which emperor was captured by the Persians in 260 CE?
questions.explanation: Valerian was captured by Shapur I, the first emperor taken prisoner by a foreign enemy.

questions.prompt: Why did prices soar during the crisis?

options.label: Coins held less and less silver

questions.explanation: Emperors cut the silver in the denarius, so each coin was worth less and prices rose.

questions.prompt: From Level 55: what had 69 CE revealed that the third century showed again?

options.label: Emperors had to be born in Rome
Armies could make and unmake emperors

questions.explanation: In both periods, armies raised their own commanders to the throne and removed others.

levels.title: Diocletian Divides the Empire
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Diocletian's reforms and the Tetrarchy.
levels.summary: Diocletian ended the crisis in 284 CE with four emperors, smaller provinces and price controls, then retired to his palace at Split.

cards.headline: One emperor wasn’t enough. Diocletian tried four.
cards.body: After half a century of murdered emperors, Diocletian’s fix was bold. If one ruler can’t guard everything, hire more rulers.

cards.headline: Rule of four
cards.body: Diocletian became emperor in 284 CE and ended the half century of crisis. His big idea was the Tetrarchy, “rule of four”: two senior emperors, called Augusti, and two junior ones, called Caesars. With four emperors, one could be near every threatened frontier. The junior Caesars also gave the empire a planned succession. That fixed an old problem: Rome never had a fixed law of succession, so every emperor had to pick his own heir. Now the next emperors were lined up in advance.
cards.callout: Tetrarchy: two Augusti and two Caesars

cards.headline: Smaller pieces, fixed prices
cards.body: Diocletian also split the provinces into smaller units and separated civil from military command, so the man running a province was no longer the man leading its troops. Then he took on inflation. In 301 CE his Edict on Maximum Prices tried to stop it by fixing prices by law. It failed. It turns out you can’t order a price to stay put.

cards.fact: Diocletian did what no emperor had done: he retired.
cards.context: In 305 CE he stepped down voluntarily, the first Roman emperor to do so, and moved to his palace at Split, in modern Croatia. After an age when most emperors left office by being killed, this one simply packed up and left.
